questions.stem: What is a price ceiling?

options.text: A minimum price set by the government.
A maximum price set by the government.
The equilibrium price in the market.
The price at which goods are freely traded.

questions.explanation: A price ceiling is the maximum price set by the government to make goods affordable. It is typically set below the equilibrium price.

distractorRationale.a: This describes a price floor, not a ceiling.
distractorRationale.c: The equilibrium price is the natural market price without intervention.
distractorRationale.d: This option describes a free market scenario without controls.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a likely effect of setting a price ceiling below the equilibrium price?

options.text: Surplus of goods in the market.
Shortage of goods in the market.

questions.explanation: A price ceiling set below the equilibrium price results in a shortage because the lower price increases demand while discouraging supply.

distractorRationale.a: A surplus occurs when the price floor is above equilibrium.
distractorRationale.c: Producer profits typically decrease due to reduced prices.
distractorRationale.d: Consumer demand usually increases, not decreases, due to lower prices.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of a price floor?

options.text: To make goods affordable for consumers.
To ensure producers receive a fair price.
To reduce the supply of goods.

questions.explanation: A price floor is set above the equilibrium price to ensure that producers receive a fair price for their goods, preventing them from selling at a loss.

distractorRationale.a: Price floors are not designed to make goods affordable for consumers.
distractorRationale.c: Price floors typically increase supply by ensuring higher prices.
distractorRationale.d: Consumer demand may decrease due to higher prices, not increase.

questions.stem: What is a price floor?

options.text: A minimum price set by the government
A maximum price set by the government
The market price determined by supply and demand
A price that fluctuates based on consumer preference

questions.explanation: A price floor is a minimum price set by the government for a particular good or service. It is intended to ensure that prices do not fall below a level that would threaten the financial viability of producers.

distractorRationale.b: This describes a price ceiling, not a floor.
distractorRationale.c: This describes a market-determined price, not a government-imposed price.
distractorRationale.d: This does not relate to the concept of price floors.

questions.stem: What is one effect of a price ceiling set below the equilibrium price?
questions.explanation: When a price ceiling is set below the equilibrium price, it typically results in a shortage of the good because the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied at that price. This imbalance can lead to long lines and waiting lists for consumers.

distractorRationale.a: A price ceiling usually does not increase supply; it restricts prices.
distractorRationale.c: Price ceilings disrupt equilibrium rather than stabilize it.
distractorRationale.d: Demand does not typically decrease; rather, it increases due to lower prices.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about price floors is true?

questions.explanation: Price floors are typically set above the equilibrium price to ensure that prices do not fall too low, which can harm producers. This can lead to surpluses in the market as supply exceeds demand at that price.

distractorRationale.b: This describes a price ceiling, not a floor.
distractorRationale.c: Price floors do affect the market by creating surpluses.
distractorRationale.d: Price floors can apply to essential goods, not just luxury items.

questions.stem: What happens when a price floor is implemented?

options.text: It leads to a decrease in supply.
It can cause a surplus of goods.

questions.explanation: When a price floor is implemented, particularly above the equilibrium price, it can lead to a surplus of goods because the price is artificially high, leading to an excess supply that exceeds consumer demand at that price.

distractorRationale.a: Supply does not necessarily decrease; it may increase due to higher prices.
distractorRationale.c: Price competition can still exist below the floor.
distractorRationale.d: Consumer choices may not necessarily reduce; it depends on the market.
